set.detail:
Hannibal, son of Hamilcar Barca, was born in 247 and taken to Spain at nine after swearing at the altar never to be a friend of Rome, a story he told Antiochus III himself (Polybius 3.11). He grew up in the camps of Hamilcar and Hasdrubal, married an Iberian, Imilce of Castulo, and was acclaimed commander by the army in 221 at 25. After campaigns against the Olcades and Vaccaei, he besieged Saguntum (219), provoking the war he had perhaps long planned.

In 218 he marched from New Carthage across the Pyrenees, the Rhône and the Alps, arriving in Italy with 20,000 infantry and 6,000 cavalry. In three years he won at the Ticinus, the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae, killing perhaps 100,000 Romans and allies, and won over Capua and much of the south. His strategy was political: to break Rome's Italian alliance by freeing allied prisoners and offering autonomy. It failed because the Latin colonies and central Italy stayed loyal and Rome refused to negotiate. For thirteen more years he fought in southern Italy, taking Tarentum (212), winning at Herdonia twice and at the Silarus, marching to Rome's gates (211), but losing Capua, Syracuse and, with his brother Hasdrubal's death at the Metaurus (207), his hopes of reinforcement. Recalled to Africa in 203, he was beaten by Scipio at Zama in 202.

As suffete in 196 he reformed Carthaginian finances and curbed the oligarchic court of 104, then fled in 195 to Antiochus III, advising him to invade Italy. He commanded a Seleucid fleet defeated by the Rhodians off Side (190), escaped after Apamea to Crete and Bithynia, and took poison at Libyssa in 183 when Prusias was about to surrender him to Flamininus. Polybius admired his ability to keep a polyglot army together for sixteen years without mutiny; Livy credited him with great virtues and 'inhuman cruelty, perfidy worse than Punic'. Modern debate centres on his failure to march on Rome after Cannae, the realism of his Italian strategy, and the extent to which the war was his personal project or Carthaginian state policy. His Greek companions Silenus and Sosylus wrote histories of his campaigns, now lost, which reached Polybius.

scholarship: Lancel, Hannibal (1998)
Hoyos, Hannibal's Dynasty (2003)
Seibert, Hannibal (1993)
Goldsworthy, The Fall of Carthage (2000)

set.detail:
Publius Cornelius Scipio, born in 236, son of the consul of 218, saved his wounded father at the Ticinus at 17 (Polybius' version, from Laelius), survived Cannae as a military tribune and, according to Livy, forced young nobles at Canusium who talked of leaving Italy to swear loyalty at sword point. He was curule aedile in 213 (Livy names Marcus Cornelius Cethegus as his colleague; Polybius tells of a joint candidacy with his brother Lucius), and in 210, aged about 25, was elected by the people to the Spanish command with proconsular imperium, though he had held no higher office.

In Spain he took New Carthage by a bold strike across the lagoon (209), defeated Hasdrubal Barca at Baecula (208), and destroyed Carthaginian power at Ilipa (206), where he reversed his tactical dispositions to devastating effect. He won over Masinissa and visited Syphax in Africa. Consul in 205 against the opposition of Fabius Maximus, he prepared the African invasion from Sicily with the disgraced Cannae legions and volunteers, landed in 204, burned the camps of Syphax and Hasdrubal near Utica (203), won at the Great Plains and defeated Hannibal at Zama (202), dictating peace in 201 and taking the cognomen Africanus.

After the war he was censor (199), princeps senatus, consul again (194), and in 190 accompanied his brother Lucius as legate against Antiochus III, who returned his captured son without ransom. The trials of the Scipios, led by Cato and the Petillii (187-184), forced him into retirement at Liternum, where he died in 183, asking to be buried there rather than in ungrateful Rome. Polybius (10.2-5) portrays him as a calculating rationalist who exploited belief in his divine inspiration; Livy and later tradition elaborated his piety, his visits to Jupiter's temple, his continence towards captive women and the legend of his divine birth. He was the first Roman to dominate politics through personal charisma and military success, a precursor of the great men of the late Republic, and his family (through his daughter Cornelia and adoptive grandson Scipio Aemilianus) remained central to Roman politics. A bronze bust from Herculaneum and coins have been attributed to him without certainty.

scholarship: Scullard, Scipio Africanus: Soldier and Politician (1970)
Gruen, The Fall of the Scipios (1995)
Hoyos, Hannibal's Dynasty (2003)

set.detail:
Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus, born about 280 into the patrician Fabii, was nicknamed Verrucosus for a wart on his lip and Ovicula ('little sheep') as a mild child. He was consul five times (233, 228, 215, 214, 209), censor (230), dictator at least twice (221 and 217), and an augur for 62 years. In 233 he triumphed over the Ligurians and dedicated a temple to Honos; in 218 he may have led the embassy that declared war on Carthage.

After Trasimene, elected prodictator in 217, he devised the strategy of attrition: avoiding battle, shadowing Hannibal on high ground, cutting off foraging parties and protecting the allied cities. It earned him the scorn of the army and the people, who called him Hannibal's paedagogus, and led to the unprecedented Lex Metilia granting equal power to his master of horse Minucius, whom Fabius then rescued. After Cannae, his approach became Roman policy. As consul in 215 and 214 he operated in Campania, retaking Casilinum. In 209, consul for the fifth time at about 70, he recaptured Tarentum by treachery, and when a Tarentine asked what should be done with the city's statues of the gods, replied 'leave the Tarentines their angry gods'; he did take a colossal Hercules by Lysippus for the Capitol.

He opposed Scipio's plan to invade Africa in 205, arguing that Hannibal should be defeated first in Italy and warning of the fate of Regulus; Livy gives the speeches. He died in 203, just after Hannibal left Italy. Ennius' line 'unus homo nobis cunctando restituit rem' made him the model of patient statesmanship, and Cicero (De senectute) presented him as an ideal elder statesman. His son, consul 213, predeceased him; Fabius delivered the funeral speech himself, which was still read in Cicero's time. Plutarch paired him with Pericles. Modern historians debate how far the Fabian strategy was a coherent doctrine or a response to circumstances, and how far Fabius' later reputation was shaped by his descendant Fabius Pictor and the Fabian family tradition. The term 'Fabian' has entered modern political vocabulary.

scholarship: Erdkamp, Polybius, Livy and the Fabian Strategy, AncSoc 23 (1992)
Beck, Karriere und Hierarchie (2005)

set.detail:
Marcus Claudius Marcellus, born about 268, served in the First Punic War and as a young man saved his brother in battle in Sicily. Consul in 222, he won the spolia opima at Clastidium by killing the Insubrian king Viridomarus in single combat, the third and last Roman to do so, and triumphed over the Insubres. He was consul five times (222, 215 suffect but abdicated after a flaw in the auspices, 214, 210, 208) and became known as the 'sword of Rome' to Fabius' 'shield' (Posidonius, via Plutarch).

After Cannae, he took command of the remnants at Canusium and then held Nola, repulsing Hannibal three times (216, 215, 214), Rome's first successes after the disaster. In 214 he went to Sicily, where he stormed Leontini and besieged Syracuse by land and sea (213-212), held at bay by Archimedes' engines; he took the city in 212 by surprise during a festival, defeated the Carthaginian relief army, and took Achradina and Ortygia. Archimedes was killed against his orders. He brought to Rome so many works of Greek art that Livy and Polybius date from his triumph the beginning of Roman admiration for Greek art and the decline of traditional austerity. The Senate denied him a full triumph because his army remained in Sicily; he triumphed on the Alban Mount and celebrated an ovation (211).

The Syracusans accused him before the Senate in 210, but then accepted him as patron. As consul in 210 he fought Hannibal at Numistro, recaptured Salapia, and in 209 fought at Canusium. In 208, consul for the fifth time at about 60, he was ambushed while reconnoitring a hill between Venusia and Bantia and killed; Hannibal gave him honourable burial and sent his ashes to his son in a silver urn. Plutarch paired him with Pelopidas. His reputation for boldness contrasted with Fabius' caution, though both shared the strategy of attrition after 216. His temple of Honos and Virtus was dedicated by his son in 205, and his descendants, including the nephew of Augustus, kept his memory alive.

scholarship: Eckstein, Senate and General (1987)
Flower, The Tradition of the Spolia Opima, ClAnt 19 (2000)
McDonnell, Roman Manliness (2006)

set.detail:
Marcus Porcius Cato, born in 234 at Tusculum into a plebeian family of farmers, served as a young soldier in the Second Punic War, at Capua, Tarentum and the Metaurus, and was introduced to Roman politics by the patrician Lucius Valerius Flaccus. Quaestor in 204 under Scipio in Sicily, he quarrelled with him over expenses and, returning via Sardinia, brought Ennius to Rome. Aedile (199), praetor in Sardinia (198), where he expelled usurers, and consul with Flaccus in 195, he spoke unsuccessfully against the repeal of the Lex Oppia and then conducted a brutal and successful campaign in Hispania Citerior, for which he triumphed. In 191, as military tribune under Glabrio, he decided the battle of Thermopylae by outflanking the Aetolians.

He was the most famous prosecutor of his day: he attacked Glabrio (189), the Scipios (187-184), Minucius Thermus, and many others, and was himself prosecuted 44 times without being convicted. His censorship of 184 with Flaccus was a byword for severity: he expelled senators, taxed luxury, cut illegal water connections, and built the Basilica Porcia. In 167 he defended the Rhodians; in 155 he urged the expulsion of the Athenian philosophers; from 153 he demanded the destruction of Carthage. In 149, in his last year, he spoke against Galba.

Cato was also the founder of Latin prose literature: his De agri cultura is the oldest complete Latin prose work; his Origines, the first Latin history of Rome and Italy; his speeches, over 150 of which Cicero knew, were models of early Latin eloquence; he also wrote a work on medicine and maxims for his son. He was hostile to Greek culture in public but learned Greek and used Greek sources. His second marriage, at 80, to the daughter of his client Salonius, produced a son, ancestor of Cato the Younger. Plutarch's Life, Nepos' brief biography and Cicero's idealised portrait in De senectute shaped his image as the stern defender of tradition. Astin's study shows a more complex figure, a novus homo who used tradition as a weapon in aristocratic competition, and a pragmatic statesman.

scholarship: Astin, Cato the Censor (1978)
Gruen, Culture and National Identity in Republican Rome (1992)
Sciarrino, Cato the Censor and the Beginnings of Latin Prose (2011)

set.detail:
Publius Cornelius Scipio Aemilianus Africanus Numantinus, born about 185, was the second son of Lucius Aemilius Paullus and was adopted by Publius Cornelius Scipio, son of Africanus. He fought at Pydna at 17, was befriended by Polybius, who became his mentor (Polybius 31.23-30 describes their friendship), and inherited Perseus' library. In 151, as military tribune in Spain under Lucullus, he killed a Celtiberian champion in single combat and won the mural crown at Intercatia. In 149, as military tribune in Africa, he saved Roman troops at Nepheris and won the respect of both armies.

In 147, though only standing for the aedileship and under the legal age, he was elected consul by popular demand, given Africa by law, restored discipline, captured Megara, blockaded Carthage and in spring 146 took and destroyed the city, weeping over it and quoting Homer to Polybius. He took the cognomen Africanus. Censor in 142 with the lax Mummius, he took a severe line on morals and at the lustrum prayed that the gods preserve rather than increase Roman power (Valerius Maximus 4.1.10). In 140-139 he led an embassy to the East with Panaetius. Elected consul again in 134 in breach of the law, he took Numantia after an eight-month siege (133) and took the name Numantinus.

He was the centre of a group of friends interested in Greek culture, including Laelius, Polybius, Panaetius, Terence and Lucilius, which Cicero idealised as the 'Scipionic Circle' (modern scholars doubt its coherence). Married to Sempronia, sister of the Gracchi, he approved of the killing of Tiberius Gracchus, quoting Homer ('so perish anyone else who does such things'). In 129 he defended the Italian allies against the Gracchan land commission; shortly afterwards he was found dead in his bed, the morning he was to speak on the issue. Suspicion fell on his wife, Cornelia, Carbo and others; no investigation was held. Cicero made him the main speaker of De re publica and the dreamer of the Somnium Scipionis.

scholarship: Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)
Zetzel, Cicero and the Scipionic Circle, HSCP 76 (1972)

set.detail:
Philip V, son of Demetrius II, born in 238, became king of Macedon at 17 in 221 on the death of his guardian Antigonus Doson. In the Social War (220-217) at the head of the Hellenic alliance against the Aetolians, he won brilliant victories, including the sack of Thermum, and was hailed as the 'darling of Greece' (Polybius). After making peace at Naupactus in 217, he turned west under the influence of Demetrius of Pharos, allied with Hannibal in 215, and fought the First Macedonian War against Rome, the Aetolians and Attalus I until the Peace of Phoenice (205). During these years his character changed, according to Polybius, from a generous king into a tyrant: he massacred the Messenians, sacked Thermum again, and allegedly poisoned Aratus.

After Phoenice he turned east, allegedly making a pact with Antiochus III to divide the Ptolemaic empire, seized Ptolemaic and independent cities in the Aegean and on the Hellespont, was mauled by the Rhodians and Attalids at Chios (201), and besieged Abydos (200). The Rhodian, Attalid and Athenian appeals brought Roman intervention. In the Second Macedonian War (200-197), he held the Aous gorge but was defeated at Cynoscephalae (197) by Flamininus, and by the peace of 196 lost his possessions outside Macedonia, his fleet and 1,000 talents, and gave his son Demetrius as a hostage.

In his last years, he cooperated with Rome against Nabis and Antiochus, but rebuilt Macedonian strength: he reformed finances, opened new mines, resettled Thracians in Macedonia, and consolidated control of the Thracian coast, which brought complaints to Rome (the Maronea massacre). His family tragedy, the poisoning of his younger son Demetrius in 180 on charges forged by his elder son Perseus, darkened his final years; Polybius saw it as divine punishment. He died at Amphipolis in 179. His coins, with a bearded portrait, are among the finest Hellenistic royal portraits. Walbank's biography established the modern view of a gifted but erratic king who reacted to circumstances rather than following a grand design.

scholarship: Walbank, Philip V of Macedon (1940)
Hammond and Walbank, A History of Macedonia III (1988)
Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)

set.detail:
Antiochus III, son of Seleucus II, born about 242, became king in 223 at 18 after his brother Seleucus III was murdered. His early reign was a struggle to hold the empire together: he crushed the satrap Molon in Media (220), was defeated by Ptolemy IV at Raphia (217) in the Fourth Syrian War, and besieged his cousin Achaeus, who had declared himself king in Asia Minor, at Sardis (215-213). From 212 to 205 he led an expedition to the eastern satrapies (the anabasis), forcing the submission of Xerxes of Armenia, Arsaces II of Parthia and Euthydemus of Bactria, and crossing the Hindu Kush to the Indian king Sophagasenus. On his return, he took the title 'Great King' (megas), and the Greeks called him Antiochus the Great.

In the Fifth Syrian War, after the death of Ptolemy IV, he won Coele-Syria and Judaea at Panium (200), then expanded into Asia Minor and Thrace, rebuilding Lysimachia (196) and claiming the inheritance of Seleucus I in Europe. This led to a cold war with Rome over the status of the Greek cities and his presence in Europe (196-192). He gave refuge to Hannibal (195) and married his daughter Cleopatra to Ptolemy V (194/3). Invited by the Aetolians, he landed in Greece in 192 with too few troops, was defeated at Thermopylae (191), lost his fleet at Myonessus and the Eurymedon (190), and was crushed at Magnesia (190/189). By the treaty of Apamea (188) he lost everything west of the Taurus, his elephants and fleet, and paid 15,000 talents.

In 187, short of money for the indemnity, he tried to plunder the temple of Bel in Elymais and was killed by the local population. His reign was the last great period of Seleucid power: he reorganised the royal cult, with high priests for himself and his queen Laodice, and his administration is known from inscriptions in Asia Minor (Ma). Polybius criticised his later years as a decline from his early energy. Modern historians (Ma, Grainger) emphasise his skill in managing the Greek cities and the realism of his ambitions, and see his war with Rome as a miscalculation.

scholarship: Ma, Antiochos III and the Cities of Western Asia Minor (1999)
Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochos the Great (2002)
Schmitt, Untersuchungen zur Geschichte Antiochos' des Grossen (1964)

set.detail:
Masinissa, son of Gala, king of the Massylii of eastern Numidia, was born about 238 and educated, according to Appian, at Carthage. He fought for Carthage in Spain from 212, distinguishing himself as a cavalry commander, notably against the Scipios in 211. After Ilipa (206) he secretly allied with Scipio. When his father died, a succession conflict and the intervention of Syphax, king of the Masaesylii and ally of Carthage, drove him from his kingdom; he lived as a fugitive with a few horsemen until Scipio landed in Africa in 204.

He was decisive in Scipio's African campaign: at Salaeca, in the burning of the camps, at the Great Plains and in the capture of Syphax (203), after which he took Cirta. Livy's story of his marriage to Sophonisba, Hasdrubal's daughter and Syphax's wife, and her suicide by poison when Scipio demanded her surrender, became a celebrated tragedy. At Zama his 4,000 Numidian cavalry, with Laelius, decided the battle. The peace of 201 recognised him as king of all Numidia and gave him the right to recover his ancestral lands, a clause he exploited for fifty years.

With Roman acquiescence, Masinissa progressively took Carthaginian territory: the Emporia region (161), the Great Plains and Tusca region (c. 152). When Carthage finally fought back in 150, it lost, and its breach of the treaty gave Rome the pretext for the Third Punic War. He supported Rome in Macedonia and Spain with troops, elephants and grain. Polybius (36.16) praised his vigour (he could ride all day at 90 and fathered a son at 86) and credited him with transforming Numidia from nomadism to agriculture and urban life, a claim partly confirmed by archaeology. He minted coins with his portrait and built a Hellenistic court at Cirta; his tomb may be the monument at El Khroub. He died in 148 aged about 90, and Scipio Aemilianus divided his royal functions among his three sons. Modern historians (Camps, Walsh) see him as the founder of the Numidian state and an astute exploiter of Roman power.

scholarship: Camps, Aux origines de la Berbérie: Massinissa (1960)
Walsh, Massinissa, JRS 55 (1965)

set.detail:
Hamilcar Barca (Barca probably meaning 'lightning'), born about 275, took command in Sicily in 247, in the eighteenth year of the First Punic War. With a small army, he seized the height of Heircte near Panormus (247-244), with its own anchorage, from which he raided the Italian coast and harassed the Romans, and then moved to Eryx (244-241), where he occupied the town between the Roman garrisons on the summit and at the foot of the mountain. Polybius (1.56-58) admired his tactical skill in a war of positions, comparing him to a boxer fighting skilfully in a confined space. After the Aegates (241), he negotiated peace with Lutatius but refused to surrender his soldiers' arms, marching them down from Eryx with honour.

In the Mercenary War (241-237), after the failure of Hanno the Great, Hamilcar took command, broke out of the blockaded isthmus via the mouth of the Bagradas, defeated Spendius at the Bagradas, won over Numidian chiefs including Naravas (to whom he promised his daughter), trapped and destroyed the rebels at the Saw (the Prion) and finally, with Hanno, defeated Mathos (238). Polybius saw the 'Truceless War' as a model of the horrors of war and the leadership of Hamilcar.

In 237, embittered by the loss of Sicily and the Roman seizure of Sardinia, which Polybius regarded as the main causes of the Second Punic War, he took an army to Spain with his son-in-law Hasdrubal and his son Hannibal, after making the boy swear eternal hostility to Rome. In nine years he conquered southern and eastern Spain, founded Akra Leuke, and exploited the silver mines. He died in 229 or 228, drowned while retreating across a river during the siege of Helice, covering the escape of his sons. Fabius Pictor and later Roman tradition presented him as the architect of a Barcid plan of revenge, an interpretation Polybius accepted in part; modern historians (Hoyos) see a pragmatic statesman rebuilding Carthaginian power. His family, the Barcids, dominated Carthaginian politics for thirty years.

scholarship: Hoyos, Hannibal's Dynasty (2003)
Hoyos, Truceless War (2007)

set.detail:
Hasdrubal, second son of Hamilcar, born about 245, accompanied his father to Spain and was left in command there when Hannibal marched to Italy in 218, with an army of about 15,000 men and a fleet. In 217 he lost a naval battle at the mouth of the Ebro to Gnaeus Scipio. In 215, ordered to march to Italy, he was defeated by the Scipio brothers at Ibera (Dertosa) when his Spanish troops broke, a defeat that kept him in Spain. He was then recalled to Africa to fight Syphax, and on his return, with Mago and Hasdrubal son of Gisco, he destroyed the armies of the Scipio brothers in 211 in the upper Baetis valley, bribing their Celtiberian mercenaries to leave.

In 211 Livy says he escaped from Claudius Nero at the Lapides Atri by trickery. Defeated by Scipio at Baecula in 208, he withdrew with most of his Carthaginian troops, elephants and treasury and marched north-west, crossing the Pyrenees by the western route and wintering in Gaul, where he recruited Gauls. In spring 207 he crossed the Alps, more easily than his brother, since the Alpine peoples now knew the Carthaginians' intentions, and descended into Italy with about 30,000 men. After besieging Placentia unsuccessfully, he marched down the Adriatic coast.

His letters to Hannibal, proposing a meeting in Umbria, were captured, and Claudius Nero marched north to join Livius Salinator. At the Metaurus, Hasdrubal was trapped and defeated, and died fighting, charging the Roman lines when he saw that all was lost. Polybius (11.2) praised his death as worthy of his father. Nero threw his head into Hannibal's camp. Livy (27.49) also praises him. His failure to join Hannibal ended Carthaginian hopes in Italy. Modern historians (Lazenby) consider his march from Spain to Italy a remarkable achievement, and his defeat at the Metaurus one of the decisive battles of the war, although some criticise his slowness in Gaul and his decision to besiege Placentia.

scholarship: Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
Hoyos, Hannibal's Dynasty (2003)

set.detail:
Polybius, son of Lycortas, was born about 200 at Megalopolis in Arcadia into a leading family of the Achaean League. As a young man he carried the ashes of Philopoemen to burial (182), wrote a lost biography of him, and was elected hipparchus (cavalry commander) of the League in 170/169, during the Third Macedonian War, when he offered the League's support to the consul Quintus Marcius Philippus. After Pydna, he was among the 1,000 Achaeans deported to Italy on Callicrates' denunciation (167). Through his friendship with Scipio Aemilianus and Fabius Maximus Aemilianus, he was allowed to stay in Rome, where he became Scipio's mentor and companion, hunting with him and discussing politics.

He helped the Seleucid hostage Demetrius escape from Rome (162), returned to Greece with the surviving Achaean detainees in 150, and accompanied Scipio to the siege of Carthage (147-146), witnessing its destruction and exploring the African coast and possibly the Atlantic with a fleet provided by Scipio. After the sack of Corinth (146), he helped settle Greek affairs and was honoured with statues in Achaean cities. He may have accompanied Scipio to Numantia (134-133) and written a monograph on the Numantine War. He died at about 82, reportedly after a fall from a horse.

His Histories, in 40 books, covered the period from 264 (with an introduction) to 146, with the central aim of explaining how Rome conquered almost the whole inhabited world in less than 53 years (220-167). Books 1-5 survive complete, the rest in fragments and excerpts. He insisted on 'pragmatic history', the importance of autopsy, travel and documents (he used treaties, inscriptions and Hannibal's Lacinium inscription), and criticised his predecessors (Timaeus, Phylarchus, Fabius Pictor). His book 6 analyses the Roman constitution as a mixed constitution, a key text for later political thought (Machiavelli, Montesquieu, the American founders). His concept of symploke, the interconnection of events across the Mediterranean, makes him the first universal historian of the Roman age. He is the main source for Livy's books on the third and second centuries.

scholarship: Walbank, Polybius (1972)
Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius (1957-1979)
Champion, Cultural Politics in Polybius's Histories (2004)

set.detail:
Titus Quinctius Flamininus, born about 229, served as military tribune under Marcellus (208), was propraetor at Tarentum (205-204), and served as a commissioner for reinforcing the colony of Venusia (200). In 198, under 30, he was elected consul without having been praetor, against tribunician opposition, and given command against Philip V. Fluent in Greek and admired by the Greeks, he combined diplomacy and war: he forced the Aous gorge (198), won over the Achaean League, negotiated with Philip at Nicaea, and won the decisive victory of Cynoscephalae (197).

In 196, at the Isthmian Games, he proclaimed the freedom of the Greeks, a highly popular act that won him cult honours: games (Titeia) and priests were established in his honour at Chalcis, and Plutarch preserves a hymn sung in his honour there. A gold stater with his portrait, struck in Greece, is one of the earliest coin portraits of a living Roman. In 195 he led a coalition against Nabis of Sparta, besieging Sparta but leaving Nabis on the throne; in 194 he evacuated the last Roman garrisons and celebrated a three-day triumph, displaying 1,200 Roman prisoners from Cannae ransomed by the Achaeans.

In the following years he was the Senate's chief expert on Greek affairs: he negotiated with Antiochus' envoys in 193, campaigned diplomatically in Greece in 192-191, intervened to save the Aetolians at Naupactus and the Messenians from Achaean domination. Censor in 189 with Marcellus, he chose Africanus as princeps senatus. His reputation suffered from his brother Lucius' expulsion from the Senate by Cato (184) and from his role in 183, when as envoy to Prusias I he demanded the surrender of Hannibal, leading to Hannibal's suicide. He died in 174. Plutarch paired him with Philopoemen. Modern historians (Badian) have debated his motives, seeing a combination of personal ambition, philhellenism and Roman political interest; his policy of 'freedom of the Greeks' laid the foundations of Roman hegemony in Greece.

scholarship: Badian, Titus Quinctius Flamininus: Philhellenism and Realpolitik (1970)
Pfeilschifter, Titus Quinctius Flamininus (2005)

set.detail:
Lucius Aemilius Paullus, born about 229, son of the consul killed at Cannae, was curule aedile in 193 (building the Porticus Aemilia), praetor in Hispania Ulterior in 191-189, where he was defeated by the Lusitanians at Lyco (190) but won a great victory the following year and issued the Lascuta decree freeing the 'slaves of the Hastenses' (the earliest surviving Latin document from Spain). Consul in 182 and proconsul in 181, he defeated the Ingauni Ligurians and triumphed. He was an augur for over 30 years, famous for his scrupulous observance of ritual.

In 168, consul for the second time at about 60, he was given command against Perseus after three years of failure. He restored discipline, outmanoeuvred Perseus via Pythium and won the battle of Pydna (22 June 168) in about an hour, ending the Antigonid monarchy. He toured Greece, visiting Delphi, where he converted a pillar intended for a statue of Perseus into his own monument, and Olympia, where he was moved by Phidias' Zeus. At Amphipolis he organised the settlement of Macedonia into four republics and held magnificent games. On the Senate's orders, he sacked 70 towns in Epirus, selling 150,000 people into slavery. His triumph in 167 brought so much money that the tributum was suspended; but his two younger sons died in the days around the triumph, a tragedy he presented as the price of Rome's good fortune.

Censor in 164, he died in 160 after a long illness. His funeral games were given by his sons Fabius Maximus Aemilianus and Scipio Aemilianus, adopted into other families, with the first performance of Terence's Adelphoe. Polybius (31.22) emphasises his poverty: his estate was barely enough to repay his widow's dowry, although he had controlled the Macedonian treasure. He gave Perseus' library to his sons. Plutarch paired him with Timoleon. He represents for Roman tradition the ideal of the incorruptible general and philhellene aristocrat, though the sack of Epirus shows the other side of Roman power. Modern scholars have studied his Delphic monument as the first Roman historical relief.

scholarship: Reiter, Aemilius Paullus: Conqueror of Greece (1988)
Kähler, Der Fries vom Reiterdenkmal des Aemilius Paullus in Delphi (1965)

set.detail:
Gaius Flaminius, a novus homo born about 275, was the most controversial Roman politician of the period between the Punic Wars. As tribune of the plebs in 232, he carried, against the opposition of the Senate and even his own father, a plebiscite distributing the ager Gallicus Picenus, land confiscated from the Senones south of Ariminum, to Roman citizens in individual allotments (viritim). Polybius (2.21) blamed this law for the beginning of the moral decline of the Roman people and for provoking the Gallic invasion of 225, a view derived from the senatorial tradition represented by Fabius Pictor.

In 227 he was one of the first two praetors sent to govern a province, Sicily, where he was remembered fondly. As consul in 223, with Publius Furius Philus, he crossed the Po and defeated the Insubres on the Adda; the Senate, citing unfavourable omens, ordered him to return, but he opened the letter only after the battle, and the people granted him a triumph against the Senate's wishes. Censor in 220, he built the Via Flaminia, from Rome to Ariminum, and the Circus Flaminius in the Campus Martius. In 218 he was the only senator to support the Lex Claudia restricting senatorial trade.

Elected consul for 217 by the people, he left Rome secretly without performing the customary ceremonies on the Capitol, fearing that his enemies would delay him with religious obstacles, and took up command at Arretium. In June 217, pursuing Hannibal, he was ambushed at Lake Trasimene and killed with about 15,000 men by an Insubrian horseman named Ducarius. The ancient tradition, notably Livy (21.63, 22.3), presents him as reckless and impious, ignoring omens. Modern historians have rehabilitated him to some extent, seeing him as a reformer who championed the interests of small farmers and the people, a precursor of the Gracchi, whose defeat was due to Hannibal's skill rather than recklessness. His son, consul in 187, built a road from Bononia to Arretium.

scholarship: Yavetz, The Policy of Gaius Flaminius and the Plebiscitum Claudianum, Athenaeum 40 (1962)
Feig Vishnia, State, Society and Popular Leaders in Mid-Republican Rome (1996)

set.detail:
Hiero, son of Hierocles, born about 306 into a Syracusan family that claimed descent from the tyrant Gelon, served under Pyrrhus in Sicily (278-276). After Pyrrhus left, the Syracusan army elected him general; he consolidated his position by marrying the daughter of Leptines, a leading citizen, and by defeating the Mamertines at the Longanus river (c. 269 or 265), after which he was acclaimed king. In 264 he allied with Carthage to besiege Messana but was defeated by Appius Claudius Caudex and withdrew. In 263, when the Romans marched on Syracuse with four legions, he made peace and became Rome's ally, a relationship he maintained for nearly 50 years.

His kingdom covered south-eastern Sicily, with Syracuse, Leontini, Megara, Akrai, Helorus, Netum and Tauromenium. He supplied Rome with grain, siege engines and money during both Punic Wars, sending in 216 grain and a golden Victory weighing 320 pounds. His tax law, the lex Hieronica, organised the tithe on grain in such detail that Rome retained it for the province of Sicily, as Cicero's Verrines show. He built extensively in Syracuse: a great altar 200 metres long, the enlarged theatre, which bears inscriptions of his queen Philistis and his son Gelon, and the giant ship Syracusia, designed with Archimedes' help, which he sent as a gift to Ptolemy III loaded with grain.

Hiero was a patron of Archimedes, a relative, who designed defensive engines and solved problems for him, according to tradition, including the famous problem of the gold crown (Vitruvius). Theocritus addressed his Idyll 16 to him. He helped the Rhodians after the earthquake of 227/226. He died in 215 at over 90, after 54 years of rule, having outlived his son Gelon. His grandson Hieronymus abandoned the Roman alliance, leading to the siege and fall of Syracuse (213-212). Polybius (7.8) praised his moderation, his long reign without killing, exiling or harming any citizen. Modern historians see his reign as the last flowering of Greek Sicily and a model of a Hellenistic client king of Rome.

scholarship: De Sensi Sestito, Gerone II (1977)
Lehmler, Syrakus unter Agathokles und Hieron II (2005)
Serrati, Sicily in the Roman Republic (2000)

set.detail:
Archimedes of Syracuse, born about 287, son of the astronomer Phidias, probably studied in Alexandria, where he corresponded with mathematicians such as Conon of Samos and Eratosthenes, and was a relative or friend of Hiero II. He is considered the greatest mathematician of antiquity. His surviving works include On the Sphere and Cylinder (proving that a sphere's volume and surface are two-thirds those of the circumscribing cylinder), Measurement of a Circle (approximating pi between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7), On Conoids and Spheroids, On Spirals, Quadrature of the Parabola, On Floating Bodies (founding hydrostatics), On the Equilibrium of Planes (founding statics), The Sand-Reckoner (a system for expressing huge numbers, with the heliocentric hypothesis of Aristarchus) and The Method, a letter to Eratosthenes discovered in 1906 in a palimpsest (the Archimedes Palimpsest), revealing his use of mechanical methods and infinitesimals.

Ancient tradition credited him with many inventions: the water screw (cochlias), compound pulleys with which he moved a ship single-handed before Hiero ('give me a place to stand and I will move the earth'), a planetarium that Marcellus took to Rome, and the solution of the gold crown problem by measuring displacement in water ('eureka', Vitruvius 9 praef.). During the siege of Syracuse (213-212), his war machines, according to Polybius (8.3-7), Livy and Plutarch, included catapults for various ranges, cranes that lifted and dropped ships, and small scorpions shooting through loopholes; the story of burning mirrors appears only in later authors (Lucian, Galen, Tzetzes).

He was killed during the sack of Syracuse in 212 by a Roman soldier, against Marcellus' orders. Plutarch gives several versions of his death, the most famous being that he was absorbed in drawing a diagram in the sand. His tomb, marked by a sphere and cylinder, was found neglected by Cicero in 75. His works were preserved mainly through Byzantine manuscripts and Arabic translations, and influenced Galileo, Kepler and Newton. Modern study of the Archimedes Palimpsest, imaged with multispectral techniques from 1999, has revealed new texts, including parts of the Stomachion and The Method.

scholarship: Dijksterhuis, Archimedes (1956)
Netz and Noel, The Archimedes Codex (2007)
Jaeger, Archimedes and the Roman Imagination (2008)

set.detail:
Marcus Atilius Regulus, consul for the first time in 267, when he triumphed over the Sallentini, was elected consul again (suffect) in 256 after the death of Quintus Caedicius. With his colleague Lucius Manlius Vulso Longus, he commanded the great fleet that defeated the Carthaginians at Ecnomus and landed at Aspis (Clupea) in Africa. When Manlius returned to Rome with most of the fleet, Regulus remained with 15,500 infantry and 500 cavalry, defeated the Carthaginians at Adys, took Tunes and threatened Carthage.

Wanting to end the war before his successor arrived, he offered peace terms so harsh (evacuation of Sicily and Sardinia, release of Roman prisoners without ransom, payment of Roman war costs, an annual tribute, and a limited navy) that the Carthaginians preferred to fight. In 255, the Spartan mercenary Xanthippus reorganised the Carthaginian army and defeated Regulus at the battle of Tunes on the Bagradas plain; Regulus was captured with 500 men. Polybius (1.35) used his fate as an example of the reversal of fortune and the danger of arrogance in success.

The Roman legend, absent from Polybius but developed by Cicero, Horace (Odes 3.5) and later writers, says that around 250 the Carthaginians sent Regulus to Rome on parole to negotiate peace or an exchange of prisoners; he advised the Senate to refuse, then returned to Carthage as he had sworn, and was tortured to death, his eyelids cut off and exposed to the sun, or put in a barrel lined with nails. Diodorus (24.12) records that Regulus' widow, Marcia, tortured two Carthaginian prisoners given to her in revenge, one dying; this may have prompted the creation of the legend to justify the cruelty. Modern historians consider the embassy legendary and think Regulus died in captivity, perhaps of natural causes. The legend made him a model of fides and patriotic sacrifice in Roman tradition, cited by Cicero (De officiis 3.99-115) as the prime example of keeping an oath.

scholarship: Mix, Marcus Atilius Regulus: Exemplum Historicum (1970)
Lazenby, The First Punic War (1996)

set.detail:
Gaius Duilius, a novus homo, was consul in 260 with Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio, and initially commanded the land army in Sicily. When Scipio was captured with his squadron at Lipara, Duilius took over the newly built fleet of about 100 ships equipped with the corvus, a boarding bridge. Off Mylae, on the north coast of Sicily, he defeated the Carthaginian fleet of 130 ships under Hannibal son of Gisco, capturing about 30 to 50 ships, including the flagship that had belonged to Pyrrhus. It was Rome's first naval victory. He then relieved Segesta, besieged by the Carthaginians, and took the town of Macella by storm.

He celebrated the first naval triumph in Roman history in 260. He was honoured with a column decorated with the bronze rams of captured ships (columna rostrata) in the Forum, with an inscription recording his achievements; a version of the inscription, restored in the reign of Claudius in archaising Latin, survives in the Capitoline Museums (CIL I2 25). He also received the unique privilege of being escorted home from dinner by a torch-bearer and a flute player, according to Cicero (De senectute 44) and Livy's epitome. He built a temple of Janus in the Forum Holitorium with the spoils.

He was censor in 258 and dictator for the elections in 231. His career is a typical example of the opportunities that the First Punic War created for new men. Pliny and Florus mention his monument. Modern historians debate the reliability of the inscription's figures (it claims 31 ships captured, 13 sunk, and large quantities of gold and silver) and the extent to which the corvus was his invention or that of an unknown engineer. The victory at Mylae became part of Roman national mythology, and Duilius was cited as an example of a military hero by Cicero, Tacitus and others.

scholarship: Thiel, A History of Roman Sea-Power before the Second Punic War (1954)
Kondratieff, The Column and Coinage of C. Duilius, SCI 23 (2004)

set.detail:
Perseus, born about 212, eldest son of Philip V, commanded Macedonian troops as a young man in the Second Macedonian War and against the Dardanians. His rivalry with his younger brother Demetrius, favoured by Rome after his stay as a hostage, led to the execution of Demetrius in 180, after Perseus accused him of plotting to seize the throne with Roman help, allegedly on the basis of a forged letter of Flamininus. He succeeded Philip in 179 and renewed the treaty of friendship with Rome.

In the following years he tried to rebuild Macedonian prestige in Greece through popular measures: he recalled exiles, cancelled debts, and married Laodice, daughter of Seleucus IV, while giving his sister to Prusias II of Bithynia. He gained popularity among the Greek lower classes and intervened in Thessaly, Boeotia and Aetolia. Eumenes II of Pergamon denounced him before the Senate in 172 as a threat to Rome; when Eumenes was attacked near Delphi on his way home, Perseus was blamed. Rome, after deceiving him with negotiations (Marcius Philippus' 'new wisdom'), declared war in 171.

In the Third Macedonian War (171-168), Perseus won at Callinicus (171), but did not exploit his success, offering peace on the terms of 196, which Rome refused. He was criticised by Polybius and Livy for his avarice, failing to pay Genthius the promised subsidy and dismissing Bastarnian mercenaries rather than pay them. In 168 he was defeated at Pydna by Aemilius Paullus. He fled to Samothrace with his treasure, where he surrendered to the praetor Gnaeus Octavius. Led in Paullus' triumph in 167, he was imprisoned at Alba Fucens, where he died a few years later, perhaps by starvation or sleep deprivation. His son Alexander became a clerk in Rome. Modern historians (Gruen) see him as a king unjustly portrayed by the pro-Roman tradition, whose policies were defensive rather than aggressive, and whose war was largely provoked by Roman suspicion and Eumenes' interests.

scholarship: Gruen, Class Conflict and the Third Macedonian War, AJAH 1 (1976)
Hammond and Walbank, A History of Macedonia III (1988)
Burton, Rome and the Third Macedonian War (2017)

set.detail:
Antiochus IV Epiphanes, born about 215, third son of Antiochus III, was a hostage in Rome after Apamea (188) for about twelve years, where he absorbed Roman culture: he later organised gladiatorial games in Antioch and imitated Roman magistrates by canvassing in the agora of Antioch. Released in exchange for his nephew Demetrius (c. 176/5), he lived in Athens, where he held public office, and returned to Syria after the murder of his brother Seleucus IV by Heliodorus in 175, with the support of Eumenes II and Attalus of Pergamon. He became king, at first as guardian and co-ruler of Seleucus' young son, whom he later had killed.

In the Sixth Syrian War (170-168), he defeated the Ptolemaic army at Pelusium, captured Ptolemy VI, and occupied most of Egypt. In his second invasion in 168, while besieging Alexandria, he was humiliated by the Roman envoy Popillius Laenas at Eleusis and forced to leave Egypt. On his return he sacked Jerusalem, built a fortress (the Akra), and in December 167 his officials converted the temple into a sanctuary of Zeus Olympios and banned Jewish religious practices, triggering the Maccabean revolt. In 166 he held a lavish festival at Daphne, rivalling Aemilius Paullus' games at Amphipolis, with 50,000 troops including 5,000 men armed in Roman fashion.

He died in late 164 during an expedition to the eastern provinces, after failing to plunder a temple in Elymais. Polybius (26.1) called him Epimanes ('the mad') instead of Epiphanes ('god manifest'), describing his eccentric behaviour: he roamed the streets, drank with ordinary people, and gave strange gifts. The Book of Daniel and the books of Maccabees portray him as the archetypal persecutor. Modern historians have reinterpreted his reign, seeing his religious policy in Judaea as a response to a civil conflict among Jews and a revolt, and his reign as an energetic attempt to restore Seleucid power after Apamea. He founded or refounded many cities named Antioch or Epiphania and promoted the cult of Zeus Olympios.

scholarship: Mørkholm, Antiochus IV of Syria (1966)
Gruen, Hellenism and Persecution, in Hellenistic History and Culture (1993)
Mittag, Antiochos IV. Epiphanes (2006)

set.detail:
Eumenes II Soter, son of Attalus I, born about 221, became king of Pergamon in 197. Loyal to Rome, he fought alongside the Romans against Nabis (195) and Antiochus III, playing a key role at Magnesia (190), where his cavalry routed the Seleucid left and his archers panicked the scythed chariots. At Apamea (188) he received most of Seleucid Asia Minor north of the Taurus, making Pergamon the main power in Anatolia. He fought Prusias I of Bithynia, whose fleet was commanded by Hannibal (186-183), Pharnaces I of Pontus (183-179) and the Galatians.

He was a great builder and patron of culture: the Great Altar of Pergamon, the library (second only to Alexandria's, the rivalry with which led, according to Pliny, to the development of parchment, pergamena), the theatre terrace, the stoas he donated to Athens (the Stoa of Eumenes below the Acropolis) and Delphi. He married Stratonice, daughter of Ariarathes IV of Cappadocia. His loyalty to Rome was rewarded: in 172 he went to Rome to denounce Perseus, an act that contributed to the Third Macedonian War; on his way home he was attacked and wounded by assailants at Delphi, perhaps hired by Perseus, and was believed dead, so that his brother Attalus married his wife, an episode he later forgave.

After Pydna, however, Eumenes fell under suspicion of negotiating with Perseus; when he came to Italy in 167/6 to defend himself, the Senate decreed that kings could not come to Rome and had him turned away at Brundisium. Rome encouraged his brother Attalus and declared the Galatians, whom Eumenes had defeated, autonomous (166). He died in 159 and was succeeded by Attalus II, as regent for his son Attalus III. Polybius (32.8) praised him as a king who brought his small kingdom to the level of the greatest, through his intelligence and generosity to the Greeks. Modern historians (Allen, Hansen) see his reign as the golden age of Pergamon and an example of the vulnerability of Rome's client kings.

scholarship: Allen, The Attalid Kingdom (1983)
Hansen, The Attalids of Pergamon (2nd edn 1971)
Kosmetatou, The Attalids of Pergamon, in A Companion to the Hellenistic World (2003)

set.detail:
Viriathus, a Lusitanian shepherd who became a hunter and brigand, was one of the few survivors of the massacre of the Lusitanians by Servius Sulpicius Galba in 150. In 147, when the Lusitanians, surrounded by the praetor Gaius Vetilius, were negotiating surrender, he persuaded them to fight on and was chosen as leader. He saved the army by ordering it to scatter while he held off the Romans with 1,000 horsemen, then lured Vetilius into an ambush at Tribola, where Vetilius was killed.

For eight years he waged a war of movement in Hispania Ulterior and Citerior, using his knowledge of terrain, feigned retreats and night attacks to defeat a series of Roman commanders: Gaius Plautius (146), Claudius Unimanus (145), Gaius Nigidius. He was checked by Quintus Fabius Maximus Aemilianus (145-144) but recovered, inciting the Celtiberians to rise in 143 (the beginning of the Numantine War). In 140, he trapped the army of Quintus Fabius Maximus Servilianus near Erisane and, rather than destroying it, negotiated a peace by which he was recognised as a friend of the Roman people, and the Lusitanians kept the land they held; the treaty was ratified in Rome.

In 139, Quintus Servilius Caepio, Servilianus' successor, obtained authorisation to break the treaty and bribed three of Viriathus' envoys, Audax, Ditalcus and Minurus, who murdered him in his sleep. The Senate refused to pay the assassins. His followers gave him a magnificent funeral with games; his successor Tautalus surrendered soon after. Diodorus (33.1, 33.7, 33.21a), following Posidonius, praised his simplicity, justice, and leadership: he shared the hardships of his men, kept little booty for himself, and at his wedding refused the rich food, preferring to sit on horseback. Livy's epitome calls him a 'man and general of the highest kind'. Viriathus became a national hero in Portugal and Spain. Modern historians debate whether he was a bandit chief, the leader of a social revolt of the poor, or a champion of Lusitanian independence.

scholarship: Pastor Muñoz, Viriato: la lucha por la libertad (2000)
Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)
Simon, Roms Kriege in Spanien (1962)

set.detail:
Quintus Ennius, born in 239 at Rudiae in Calabria, an Oscan-speaking area of Messapian origin with Greek culture, claimed to have 'three hearts' because he spoke Oscan, Greek and Latin. He served as a centurion in the Roman army in Sardinia, where Cato met him in 204 and brought him to Rome. There he taught Greek and adapted Greek tragedies, mainly from Euripides, for the Roman stage, living modestly on the Aventine. He became attached to the great families: he accompanied Marcus Fulvius Nobilior on his Aetolian campaign of 189, celebrating the capture of Ambracia in a play, and in 184 received Roman citizenship through Nobilior's son, who enrolled him in a colony.

His masterpiece was the Annales, an epic poem in 18 books (originally 15, extended later) narrating Roman history from the fall of Troy and the arrival of Aeneas to his own time. It was the first Latin poem in dactylic hexameters, replacing the native Saturnian verse used by Livius Andronicus and Naevius, and established a Hellenistic poetic language in Latin. In the proem he claimed that the soul of Homer had passed into him in a dream. Only about 600 lines survive in quotations. His other works included tragedies (Medea, Andromache, Thyestes), comedies, praetextae (Ambracia, Sabinae), satires, a philosophical poem Epicharmus, the Euhemerus on the origin of the gods, and the Hedyphagetica, a gourmet poem on fish.

He died in 169, shortly after the production of his Thyestes. Cicero (Brutus 78, De senectute 14) describes him in old age, bearing poverty and old age cheerfully. His statue was said to stand in the tomb of the Scipios. His epitaph claimed that he flew 'living on the lips of men'. The Annales was the national epic of Rome until Virgil's Aeneid, which borrowed from it extensively. Cicero quoted him constantly; Lucretius praised him; Quintilian compared him to venerable sacred groves. Skutsch's edition (1985) is the standard text.

scholarship: Skutsch, The Annals of Quintus Ennius (1985)
Goldberg, Constructing Literature in the Roman Republic (2005)
Elliott, Ennius and the Architecture of the Annales (2013)

set.detail:
Titus Maccius Plautus, born about 254 at Sarsina in Umbria, came to Rome, according to tradition, as a theatre worker, earned money in the theatre, lost it in trade, and worked in a mill, writing plays in his spare time (Gellius 3.3, from Varro). His name may be a nickname: Maccius suggests Maccus, the clown of Atellan farce, and Plautus 'flat-footed'. He was active from about 205 to his death, which Cicero dates to 184. About 130 comedies circulated under his name in antiquity; Varro identified 21 as certainly authentic, and these are the ones that survive, making him the earliest Latin author whose works survive complete.

His plays are adaptations of Greek New Comedy by Menander, Diphilus, Philemon and others, set in Greek cities with Greek characters, but full of Roman references, puns and allusions. Only two can be dated precisely from their production notices (didascaliae): Stichus (Ludi Plebeii of 200) and Pseudolus (Ludi Megalenses of 191, at the dedication of the temple of Magna Mater). Others are dated by internal references, such as the Miles Gloriosus (perhaps c. 205, with an allusion to Naevius' imprisonment) and Truculentus. His comedies include Amphitruo (the only mythological comedy, model for Molière), Aulularia (model for Molière's L'Avare), Menaechmi (model for Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors), Mostellaria, Rudens, Captivi and Casina.

Plautus' comedies were musical: much of the text was sung or chanted (cantica), with complex metres, and featured scheming slaves (the servus callidus), lovesick young men, greedy pimps and boastful soldiers. Fraenkel's study (Plautinisches im Plautus, 1922) showed how much Plautus transformed his Greek models, adding farce, wordplay and musical elements. Modern scholarship debates the extent of his originality and the social meaning of his plays, with their inversions of the master-slave relationship in a society increasingly dependent on slavery after the Second Punic War. His plays were performed at the expanding public games, which grew rapidly between 220 and 180. Varro, Cicero and Gellius admired his Latin; Horace criticised his metres and jokes.

scholarship: Fraenkel, Plautine Elements in Plautus (Eng. trans. 2007 of Plautinisches im Plautus, 1922)
Segal, Roman Laughter (1968)
Richlin, Slave Theater in the Roman Republic (2017)

set.detail:
Publius Terentius Afer, born in Carthage (Afer means 'the African'), perhaps about 195 or 185, came to Rome as a slave of the senator Terentius Lucanus, who educated him and freed him, according to Suetonius' biography preserved by Donatus. He became friends with young aristocrats, Scipio Aemilianus and Gaius Laelius, which led to rumours that they helped write his plays, which Terence answered ambiguously in his prologues. He produced six comedies between 166 and 160, all surviving: Andria (166), Hecyra (failed 165, again 160, successful later in 160), Heauton Timorumenos (163), Eunuchus (161, a huge success paid 8,000 sesterces), Phormio (161) and Adelphoe (160, at the funeral games of Aemilius Paullus).

His plays were adaptations of Greek New Comedy, mainly Menander, with Apollodorus of Carystus for Hecyra and Phormio. He practised contaminatio, combining scenes from two Greek plays in one, for which he was attacked by his rival, the older playwright Luscius Lanuvinus; his prologues are polemical replies to these criticisms, a new use of the prologue. Unlike Plautus, he kept the Greek atmosphere, avoided Roman allusions and broad farce, used less music, and wrote in pure, elegant conversational Latin. His characters are psychologically nuanced, and his themes include education, family relations and humanity; his line 'homo sum, humani nil a me alienum puto' ('I am human, I think nothing human alien to me', Heauton Timorumenos 77) became a motto of humanism.

After 160 he went to Greece, perhaps to collect more plays by Menander, and died in 159, at sea or in Arcadia, still young. Caesar called him a 'half-Menander' (dimidiate Menander), lacking comic force; Cicero praised his elegant Latin. His plays were studied in schools throughout antiquity and the Middle Ages: the 10th-century nun Hrotsvit of Gandersheim wrote Christian comedies modelled on him; manuscripts with illustrations of masks and scenes survive. His influence on European comedy (Molière, Shakespeare) was considerable. Modern scholars debate his relationship with the 'Scipionic Circle' and his place in the development of Roman Hellenism.

scholarship: Goldberg, Understanding Terence (1986)
Augoustakis and Traill (eds.), A Companion to Terence (2013)

set.detail:
Gaius Laelius, a novus homo born about 235, was the lifelong friend and lieutenant of Scipio Africanus. He commanded the fleet at the capture of New Carthage (209), where he blockaded the port, and was sent to Rome with the prisoners and news of victory. He fought at Baecula (208) and Ilipa (206), and was sent to Syphax and later to Masinissa. In Africa he was Scipio's most important subordinate: with Masinissa he burned the Numidian camp near Utica (203), pursued Syphax, defeated and captured him, and took Cirta. At Zama (202) he commanded the Roman cavalry on the left wing, and his return with Masinissa's Numidian cavalry against the Carthaginian rear decided the battle.

He was plebeian aedile (197), praetor in Sicily (196), and consul in 190, when he hoped to receive command against Antiochus but the Senate sent Lucius Scipio, with Africanus as legate. He governed Cisalpine Gaul, where he worked on the colonisation of the region, and served on an embassy to the Transalpine Gauls in 170. He lived long, dying perhaps after 160.

In old age, about 150, Laelius gave Polybius detailed eyewitness accounts of Scipio's life and campaigns, which Polybius used extensively and cited (10.3), notably the story of Scipio saving his father at the Ticinus and the strategy at New Carthage. Modern historians recognise that Laelius was a key source for the favourable portrait of Scipio in Polybius, and that his reminiscences shaped the Scipionic tradition. His son, Gaius Laelius Sapiens, consul in 140, was the close friend of Scipio Aemilianus, a parallel friendship across two generations that Cicero celebrated in his dialogue De amicitia, named Laelius after the son. The careers of the two Laelii show how a new family could rise through friendship with a great aristocratic house.

scholarship: Scullard, Scipio Africanus (1970)
Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius II (1967)

set.detail:
Mago, the youngest son of Hamilcar Barca, born about 243, accompanied Hannibal to Italy in 218. At the Trebia he commanded the ambush of 1,000 cavalry and 1,000 infantry hidden in a watercourse that attacked the Roman rear and decided the battle. At Cannae he commanded the centre with Hannibal, the Gallic and Spanish infantry that held the Roman legions. After Cannae he went to Carthage to report the victory and, according to Livy (23.12), poured a heap of gold rings taken from dead Roman equestrians onto the floor of the Carthaginian senate house, asking for reinforcements.

He was sent with reinforcements to Spain instead of Italy, after Hasdrubal's defeat at Dertosa (215), and fought there for ten years with his brother Hasdrubal and Hasdrubal son of Gisco. In 211 he contributed to the destruction of Publius Scipio's army. He was defeated with Hanno by Silanus in Celtiberia (207) and by Scipio at Ilipa (206). He then held Gades, failed in a raid on New Carthage, was shut out of Gades, and wintered in the Balearic Islands, where the harbour of Port Mahon in Minorca is said to bear his name (Portus Magonis).

In 205 he landed at Genua with 12,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry, recruited Ligurians and Gauls, and tried to open a second front in northern Italy. In 203 he was defeated in the territory of the Insubres by the praetor Publius Quinctilius Varus and the proconsul Marcus Cornelius Cethegus, and was seriously wounded in the thigh. Recalled to Africa, he died of his wounds on the voyage, off Sardinia, according to Livy (30.19); other traditions (Nepos, Zonaras) suggest he survived longer. The Carthaginian agronomist Mago, whose treatise was translated into Latin by order of the Senate after 146, is a different person. Modern historians see Mago as a capable commander whose efforts in Spain and Liguria were undermined by Roman superiority and the lack of support from Carthage.

scholarship: Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
Hoyos, Hannibal's Dynasty (2003)

set.detail:
Hasdrubal, called the Fair (or the Handsome), born about 270, was the son-in-law of Hamilcar Barca and a leading politician of the popular party at Carthage. Polybius (3.8), following Fabius Pictor, says he gained great influence among the people and tried to overthrow the constitution, a charge Polybius doubts. Diodorus says he was attracted to Hamilcar sexually, a hostile tradition. He played a role in the Mercenary War and accompanied Hamilcar to Spain in 237, where he was his chief lieutenant; he was sent back to Africa to suppress a Numidian revolt.

When Hamilcar died in 229 or 228, the army chose Hasdrubal as commander, confirmed by the Carthaginian people. He continued the expansion of Carthaginian power in Spain more by diplomacy than war: he married the daughter of an Iberian king and, according to Diodorus, was acclaimed supreme general by the Iberian chiefs. He founded Qart Hadasht (New Carthage, modern Cartagena) about 227, on a natural harbour, with a palace on a hill, which Polybius describes. His army, Diodorus says, numbered 50,000 infantry, 6,000 cavalry and 200 elephants. In 226 he made the Ebro treaty with Rome, agreeing not to cross the river under arms.

In 221 he was assassinated at night in his house by a Celt, a slave avenging his master's execution according to Livy, or because of a private grudge. Hannibal succeeded him. Polybius (2.36) describes him as a prudent and practical commander who did much to strengthen Carthaginian power, more by negotiation than by arms. Modern historians (Hoyos) have seen in him an architect of Carthaginian empire in Spain, comparable to Hellenistic monarchs, while emphasising that he remained a Carthaginian general accountable to the state, contrary to Fabius Pictor's view. The silver coinage of Carthago Nova, with heads interpreted by some as portraits of the Barcids, may begin under him.

scholarship: Hoyos, Hannibal's Dynasty (2003)
Lancel, Hannibal (1998)

set.detail:
Quintus Fabius Pictor, born about 270, belonged to a branch of the patrician Fabii whose cognomen came from his grandfather, Gaius Fabius Pictor, who painted the temple of Salus (304). He fought in the Gallic war of 225, probably at Telamon, and the detailed account of Roman and allied manpower in that year preserved by Polybius may derive from his history. After Cannae, in 216, the Senate sent him to consult the oracle of Delphi on how to appease the gods; he returned with instructions to make offerings and a warning against arrogance, which Livy (23.11) reports.

He wrote a history of Rome in Greek, probably completed shortly after 200, the first prose history by a Roman. It began with the legends of Aeneas, the founding of Rome by Romulus and Remus (dated to 748/7), and ran through the early Republic, briefly, to a detailed account of the First and Second Punic Wars, in which he participated. It was written in Greek, the language of historiography, perhaps to present Rome's case to the Greek world during the war against Hannibal and Philip V. A Latin version existed later, but it is unclear if it was his own.

Polybius used Fabius, along with Philinus of Agrigentum, for the First Punic War, and criticised both for bias (1.14-15): Fabius was too favourable to Rome and blamed the Second Punic War on Hasdrubal's ambition and the Barcid faction (3.8-9). Livy cites him as 'the oldest of the writers' (1.44, 2.40) and used him, directly or indirectly, for the early books and for the Second Punic War, particularly casualty figures (Trasimene, 22.7). Dionysius of Halicarnassus also used him. A painted inscription from the library of the gymnasium at Tauromenium (2nd century) summarises his account of the foundation of Rome, confirming his reputation in the Greek world. Modern historians see him as the founder of Roman historiography and the source of the senatorial perspective that shaped the tradition on the Punic Wars, including the hostile portrait of Flaminius and the favourable portrait of the Fabii.

scholarship: Badian, The Early Historians, in Dorey (ed.), Latin Historians (1966)
Frier, Libri Annales Pontificum Maximorum (1979)
Beck and Walter, Die frühen römischen Historiker I (2001)

set.detail:
Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, born about 217, served as a young man under Lucius Scipio in Asia and was sent on a famous ride from Amphissa to Pella in three days to secure Philip V's cooperation (190). As tribune of the plebs (187 or 184), though a personal enemy of the Scipios, he vetoed the imprisonment of Lucius Scipio Asiaticus out of respect for the family; tradition says that Africanus then betrothed him to his younger daughter Cornelia. As curule aedile (182) he gave lavish games at the allies' expense, which the Senate later restricted.

As praetor in Hispania Citerior (180-178), he defeated the Celtiberians in several battles, founded Gracchurris on the upper Ebro, and concluded treaties with the Celtiberian peoples that fixed their tribute, regulated military service and prohibited the founding of new fortified towns. These 'Gracchan treaties' brought peace for 25 years and were remembered by the Celtiberians with respect, so that his son Tiberius, as quaestor in 137, was able to negotiate with the Numantines. He celebrated a triumph in 178.

Consul in 177, he suppressed a major rising in Sardinia (177-176), killing or capturing 80,000, which made Sardinian slaves so cheap that 'Sardi venales' became a proverb; he triumphed in 175 and dedicated a tablet with a map of Sardinia in the temple of Mater Matuta. As censor in 169 with Gaius Claudius Pulcher, he clashed with the publicani and restricted freedmen to one urban tribe; he built the Basilica Sempronia. Consul again in 163, he went on embassies to the East (165 and 162-161). His scrupulous report of a flaw in the auspices in 163 forced the consuls of 162 to abdicate. He died about 154. His sons Tiberius and Gaius were the famous reforming tribunes; Cornelia, who refused to remarry, raised them. Cicero praised him as a model of a wise and dignified statesman.

scholarship: Richardson, The Spanish Mines and the Development of Provincial Taxation, JRS 66 (1976)
Scullard, Roman Politics 220-150 BC (1951)

set.detail:
Quintus Caecilius Metellus, born about 210, served under Aemilius Paullus at Pydna (168) and brought news of the victory to Rome. As praetor in 148, he defeated the pretender Andriscus in Macedonia, near Pydna, aided by the fleet of Attalus II, and captured him in Thrace, ending the Fourth Macedonian War. He remained in Macedonia as propraetor and in 146 defeated the Achaean general Critolaus at Scarpheia in Locris, before handing over to the consul Mummius. In 146 he celebrated a triumph and took the cognomen Macedonicus. With the spoils he built the Porticus Metelli in the Campus Martius, enclosing temples of Jupiter Stator (the first marble temple in Rome, designed by Hermodorus of Salamis) and Juno Regina, and adorned it with Lysippus' bronze group of Alexander and his companions at the Granicus, brought from Dium.

He failed several times to win the consulship before being elected for 143. In Hispania Citerior (143-142) he campaigned successfully against the Celtiberians, taking Contrebia by a ruse and showing clemency at Centobriga, where the defenders put the children of a deserter on the walls. Censor in 131, with Quintus Pompeius (the first plebeian pair), he delivered a famous speech urging citizens to marry and have children for the state, which Augustus later read to the Senate when promoting his marriage laws. When the tribune Gaius Atinius Labeo, whom he had expelled from the Senate, tried to throw him from the Tarpeian Rock, he was saved by another tribune.

He opposed Tiberius Gracchus and was an enemy of Scipio Aemilianus, but was said to have mourned him sincerely. He died about 115, at a great age, carried to his pyre by his four sons, of whom three had been consuls and the fourth was a candidate, while three daughters were married; Valerius Maximus and Pliny cite him as the example of supreme felicity. His family, the Caecilii Metelli, became the most powerful in the Senate in the late second century.

scholarship: Van Ooteghem, Les Caecilii Metelli de la République (1967)
Gruen, Roman Politics and the Criminal Courts (1968)

set.detail:
Gaius Claudius Nero, a patrician of the Claudii, served as legate of Marcellus at Nola in 214, where his cavalry failed to arrive in time to take Hannibal from the rear. As praetor in 212 and propraetor in 211 he took part in the siege of Capua. After the deaths of the Scipios in 211 he was sent to Spain with 12,000 men to restore the situation; according to Livy (26.17), he trapped Hasdrubal Barca at the Lapides Atri, but Hasdrubal escaped by false negotiations, a story many historians doubt. He was replaced by Scipio in 210 and served under Marcellus in 209.

As consul in 207, he commanded against Hannibal in southern Italy, fighting an indecisive battle at Grumentum. When his troops captured messengers bringing Hasdrubal's letters to Hannibal, he took the boldest decision of the war: without the Senate's authorisation, he marched north with 6,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry, covering about 400 kilometres in perhaps seven days, to join his colleague and enemy Marcus Livius Salinator near Sena Gallica. Together they defeated and killed Hasdrubal at the Metaurus, Nero's flanking manoeuvre deciding the battle. Nero returned south within days and had Hasdrubal's head thrown into Hannibal's camp.

In the joint triumph, Livius rode in the chariot and Nero on horseback, but the crowd's applause, Livy says, went to Nero. As censors together in 204, the two former enemies, reconciled only for the campaign, quarrelled publicly; each deprived the other of his public horse, and Livius placed 34 of the 35 tribes among the aerarii for having condemned him in 218 and then elected him. Nero later served as envoy to Egypt and the East (201-200). Horace (Odes 4.4) celebrated the Claudii Nerones for the Metaurus, in honour of the stepsons of Augustus, Tiberius and Drusus. Modern historians consider Nero's march one of the most audacious strategic moves of antiquity.

scholarship: Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
Goldsworthy, The Punic Wars (2000)

set.detail:
Publius Cornelius Scipio, consul in 218, son of Lucius Cornelius Scipio (consul 259) and father of Scipio Africanus, was assigned Spain as his province at the outbreak of the Second Punic War. Delayed by the Boian revolt in Cisalpine Gaul, he sailed to Massalia with two legions and reached the Rhône three days after Hannibal had crossed it. Realising that Hannibal was heading for Italy, he made the crucial decision to send his army on to Spain under his brother Gnaeus, while he returned to Italy to take command of the armies in the Po valley.

At the Ticinus, in late 218, his cavalry and light infantry were routed by Hannibal's Numidian and Spanish cavalry, and he was seriously wounded; according to Polybius (10.3), citing Laelius, he was saved by his 17-year-old son, the future Africanus, while another version attributed the rescue to a Ligurian slave. He withdrew across the Po to the Trebia, where his colleague Sempronius Longus, against his advice, fought and lost the battle in December 218. His decision to send his army to Spain, which Polybius praised, was strategically crucial: it prevented reinforcements from reaching Hannibal from Spain for years.

In 217 he joined his brother in Spain with 8,000 men and 20 ships, as proconsul. The Scipio brothers fought together for seven years, winning at Ibera (Dertosa, 215), recovering Saguntum (212) and winning over Spanish peoples, including through the release of the hostages at Saguntum (217) and the alliance with Syphax (213). In 211, dividing their forces to attack the three Carthaginian armies, Publius was surrounded near Castulo by Mago, Hasdrubal son of Gisco and Masinissa's Numidians, and killed with most of his army; Gnaeus was killed 29 days later. Livy (25.36) praises the two brothers as great men. Modern historians consider their Spanish campaign one of the most important achievements of the war.

scholarship: Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)

set.detail:
Philopoemen, son of Craugis, born about 253 at Megalopolis in Arcadia, was raised by the philosophers Ecdemus and Demophanes. He distinguished himself at Sellasia (222), charging the Spartan light troops without orders, a decisive act that Antigonus Doson praised. He served as a mercenary commander in Crete for about ten years, then returned to become hipparchus of the Achaean League (210/09) and strategos eight times between 208 and 183. He reformed the Achaean army, equipping it in the Macedonian manner with the sarissa phalanx, and training the cavalry; he defeated and killed the Spartan tyrant Machanidas with his own hand at Mantinea (207). At the Nemean Games, when he entered the theatre, the citharode sang the line 'he gives Greece the glory of freedom', and the crowd turned to him.

He defeated Nabis at Mount Barbosthenes (192), and after Nabis' murder brought Sparta into the Achaean League. In 188, after Spartan exiles attacked Las, he destroyed the walls of Sparta, abolished the laws of Lycurgus, and executed or expelled opponents at Compasion, an act that embittered Spartan-Achaean relations for decades. His policy towards Rome was one of independence within the alliance: he insisted on Achaean rights and resisted Roman interference, unlike Aristaenus and Callicrates, who advocated compliance.

In 183, at the age of 70, while ill with fever, he led a small force against the Messenians, who had revolted from the League, was thrown from his horse and captured, and forced to drink poison in prison. The Achaeans under Lycortas avenged him, and Polybius carried his ashes to Megalopolis. Polybius, who wrote a biography of him (lost), described him with admiration; Plutarch paired him with Flamininus and called him 'the last of the Greeks', a phrase attributed to an unnamed Roman. Pausanias records his monuments. Modern historians (Errington) see him as a skilful leader whose policies made the Achaean League the leading power in the Peloponnese but also contributed to its conflicts with Sparta and Rome.

scholarship: Errington, Philopoemen (1969)
Walbank, Polybius (1972)

set.detail:
The First Punic War (264-241) began as a dispute over Messana and became, in Polybius' words, the longest, most continuous and greatest war he knew. Its causes lie in the collapse of the Sicilian balance of power after Pyrrhus: Carthage held the west of the island, Hiero II's Syracuse the south-east, and the Mamertines of Messana, threatened by both, appealed to Rome. Rome's crossing of the Straits in 264 drew it into conflict with both Sicilian powers, but Hiero's switch to Rome in 263 left Carthage as the only enemy.

The war passed through distinct phases. On land (264-262) Rome overran eastern and central Sicily and took Agrigentum after a seven-month siege. Realising that Carthaginian sea power protected the coastal cities and threatened Italy, Rome built its first battle fleet in 261, and with the corvus won at Mylae (260), Sulci (258), Tyndaris (257) and Ecnomus (256), the largest naval battle of antiquity. The invasion of Africa (256-255) under Regulus failed at Tunes against Xanthippus' elephants and cavalry, and the rescue fleet was wrecked off Camarina. After the capture of Panormus (254) and Metellus' victory there (250), Rome besieged Lilybaeum and Drepana for nine years. The disaster at Drepana (249) and further storm losses left Rome without a fleet for six years, while Hamilcar Barca fought a guerrilla war from Heircte and Eryx. In 242 a fleet financed by private loans blockaded the western ports, and Lutatius' victory at the Aegates (241) forced Carthage to make peace.

The costs were enormous: Rome lost perhaps 600 to 700 warships, mostly to storms, and the citizen census fell from 297,797 in 252 to 241,212 in 247. Carthage lost its Sicilian possessions and paid 3,200 talents. The war transformed Rome into a naval power, created its first overseas province, and set the pattern of Roman persistence and refusal to negotiate from weakness. Its aftermath, the Mercenary War and the Roman seizure of Sardinia, created the grievances that led to the Second Punic War. Polybius' first book, based on Fabius Pictor and Philinus, is the main source, supplemented by Diodorus and Zonaras; the Egadi rams have added archaeological evidence for the final battle.

scholarship: Lazenby, The First Punic War (1996)
Goldsworthy, The Punic Wars (2000)
Hoyos (ed.), A Companion to the Punic Wars (2011)

set.detail:
The Mercenary War, also called the Libyan War or, by Polybius, the 'Truceless War' (241-237), broke out when Carthage, unable to pay its army evacuated from Sicily, concentrated about 20,000 mercenaries (Libyans, Iberians, Celts, Ligurians, Balearics and Greek half-breeds) at Sicca and tried to negotiate a reduction of their arrears. Gesco, who had commanded at Lilybaeum, came to pay them at Tunis, but the soldiers, led by the Campanian deserter Spendius and the Libyan Mathos, seized him and his treasury. The Libyan towns, burdened by heavy wartime taxation (half their crops, Polybius says), joined the revolt, providing 70,000 men and money; Utica and Hippo Acra rebelled.

Carthage was nearly destroyed. Hanno the Great, the first commander, won a battle near Utica but let the rebels recapture their camp. Hamilcar Barca, given command in 240, broke out of the blockaded isthmus via the mouth of the Bagradas and defeated Spendius. He won over the Numidian chief Naravas and offered clemency to prisoners, which led the rebel leaders to torture Gesco and 700 prisoners to death, making the war truceless. Hamilcar and Hanno quarrelled until the army chose Hamilcar. In 238 Hamilcar trapped Spendius' army at the Saw (Prion), where the starving rebels ate their prisoners and slaves before being slaughtered; Spendius was crucified before Tunis. Mathos captured and crucified the Carthaginian general Hannibal, but was finally defeated by Hamilcar and Hanno together, led in triumph and tortured to death. Utica and Hippo surrendered.

Rome behaved correctly at first, returning prisoners and allowing trade with Carthage while forbidding it with the rebels, and refusing appeals from Utica and from the mercenaries in Sardinia. But when the war ended and Carthage prepared to recover Sardinia, Rome seized the island and imposed an extra indemnity of 1,200 talents (238/7). Polybius (1.65-88) gives the only detailed account, presenting the war as a lesson in the dangers of mercenary armies and the cruelty of civil war; Flaubert's novel Salammbô (1862) made it famous. The war established Hamilcar's ascendancy and led directly to his Spanish expedition. Rebel coins inscribed LIBYON have been found.

scholarship: Hoyos, Truceless War: Carthage's Fight for Survival, 241 to 237 BC (2007)
Loreto, La grande insurrezione libica contro Cartagine (1995)
